title: Devarim: the scouts retold (Deuteronomy 1:22–46)
hook: Moses retells an old failure so it won't be repeated
carry: tell it so it won't repeat

segments.voice: Yesterday, eicha: Moses crying how can I alone, chanted in the tune of Lamentations. Did you hand someone a piece of your load? Today, the oldest failure of the journey, told again. Day four hundred eighty-five.

After a team fails at something big, there's a choice. Bury it, and hope nobody brings it up. Or hold the meeting, in the cold light of day, and walk through it step by step: what we decided, what we told ourselves, where it went wrong. It's the meeting nobody puts on the calendar gladly. Moses, standing at the Jordan with a new generation, holds it. He takes the worst moment of the forty years, the twelve scouts and the night the people wept, and he tells it again, in detail, to the children of the people who lived it.
screen: `BURY IT, OR WALK THROUGH IT.` → `THE MEETING NOBODY WANTS.` → `MOSES HOLDS IT.`

segments.voice: The path read this story back in Numbers. Twelve scouts go in, ten come back terrified, the people weep all night, and that generation is told it will die in the wilderness. Now listen to Moses' version, and notice what he changes. In his telling, the idea of scouts starts with the people. You all came to me, he says, and asked to send men ahead to search out the land. And he admits, the idea pleased me. He doesn't hide behind God's command. He puts his own yes in the story. Then he tells it plainly. The land was good, even the scouts said so, but the people murmured in their tents and said God must hate us. And then the part that's easy to forget: after the decree, a group tried to fix it by force. They marched up into the hill country without God's blessing, and the Amorites chased them, Moses says, the way bees chase. Panic, and then overcorrection. Two mistakes, not one. The rabbis tied that night of weeping to a date. The Mishnah lists it first among the disasters of the ninth of Av, and the Talmud imagines God saying: you wept for nothing that night, so it will become a night of weeping for generations. And Devarim is read on the Sabbath right before Tisha B'Av. Moses tells it so it won't be repeated. Honest about his part, honest about both mistakes.
screen: `THE IDEA PLEASED ME.` · `THE PEOPLE MURMURED IN THEIR TENTS.` · `CHASED LIKE BEES.` · `THE NIGHT OF WEEPING, THE NINTH OF AV.` · then, large: `TELL IT SO IT WON'T REPEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn from one old mistake. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a failure you'd rather not think about. Not the most painful one; one you can look at. Walk through it the way Moses does. Where did the idea come from? Where did you say yes? What did you tell yourself afterward? Did you panic, or overcorrect, or both? Find the one thing you'd tell a younger person so they wouldn't repeat it. Just one sentence. The bell holds the time.
Devarim. Words, and the book where Moses retells even the failures, so the next generation doesn't live them twice.
Your line: tell it so it won't repeat. Today, tell someone one lesson you learned the hard way, with your own part in it. Day four hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: The portion Devarim, with Moses' retelling of the scouts, is read on the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, and the Mishnah counts the decree on the wilderness generation among the calamities remembered on that fast.

fork.setup: you're Moses, retelling the scouts to a new generation forty years later. how do you tell it?
options: leave it out; why open old wounds?
tell it, including your own part and both mistakes.
fork.reveal: he tells it in full: the people asked, the idea pleased me, they murmured, and then they overcorrected and were chased like bees.

original.note: Hebrew: scouts, or spies. Deuteronomy 1:24 uses a verb from the same root: they spied it out.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rerun of the spy story from Numbers.
what it means: Moses retells his people's worst failure, his own part included, so the next generation won't repeat it.
what a scholar hears: in Deuteronomy 1:22 the people ask for scouts; in Numbers 13 God commands it. Mishnah Taanit 4:6 dates the weeping to the ninth of Av.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the 'every team / most teams' generalizations from the hook; cut 'the next morning' (Deuteronomy 1:41-44 gives no timing; that is Numbers 14:40); replaced the causal 'that's why Devarim is read before Tisha B'Av' with a plain statement; dropped the regel/foot etymology from the original-language note.
Deuteronomy 1:23 ('the thing pleased me well') and 1:44 ('chased you, as bees do') paraphrased rather than quoted; JPS wording not verified.
The contrast between Deuteronomy 1:22 (the people propose the scouts) and Numbers 13:1–2 (God commands) is noted by Rashi and others; Keeper may prefer a particular framing.
Taanit 29a: 'you wept a weeping for nothing; I will establish for you a weeping for generations'; paraphrased.
Etymology of meraglim from regel (foot) is standard; confirm.
